foundations.prompt: Which description best distinguishes a data structure from an algorithm?
options: An organization of information versus steps applied to information
A faster computer versus a slower computer
A programming language versus a memory address
foundations.explanation: A structure organizes values and relationships. An algorithm describes steps for a task; both ideas are independent of a particular language.

foundations.prompt: When n counts elements, what is the input size of [900, 2, 2, 8]?
foundations.explanation: There are four elements. Their magnitudes and whether some values repeat do not change this definition of n.

foundations.prompt: Which statement about Big O and cases is correct?
options: Big O always means worst case
Big Omega always means best case
An upper bound can describe a specified best-, average- or worst-case cost
foundations.explanation: Cases select which inputs we consider. O is an upper growth bound on that selected cost function. These are separate ideas.

foundations.prompt: Two independent loops each inspect n elements, one after the other. How does the total inspection count grow?
foundations.explanation: The counts add: n+n=2n. The constant factor two does not change linear growth. Multiplication would apply to n-by-n nested repetition.

foundations.prompt: Countdown(n) calls countdown(n−1) until zero, without guaranteed frame elimination. What is its auxiliary call-stack growth?
foundations.explanation: Up to n+1 unfinished calls can be active together. Each frame remembers a return point, so stack space grows linearly.

foundations.prompt: A largest-value algorithm has no defined output for empty input. What should its specification do?
options: Pretend the largest value is always zero
State a nonempty precondition or define an explicit empty result
Ignore empty input because one successful example proves correctness
foundations.explanation: Correctness is relative to a complete contract for allowed inputs. An empty sequence has no largest value; its behavior must be specified.

arrays.prompt: For [7, 5, 7], what does reading zero-based index 1 return?
arrays.explanation: Index 1 is the second position, whose value is 5. An index names a slot; it is not the value stored there.

arrays.prompt: With length 3 and capacity 5, which action is valid?
options: Insert at index 3, using a spare slot
arrays.explanation: The occupied indices are 0..2. Insertion permits index equal to length; reads and deletion require an existing element.

arrays.prompt: Why does in-place insertion shift elements from the end toward the insertion position?
options: To preserve values before their old slots are overwritten
To reduce every insertion to constant time
arrays.explanation: Copying from right to left protects each old value until it has been moved. Beginning insertion may still require n shifts.

searching.prompt: What permits binary search to discard half of the remaining interval?
options: Ascending order under the same comparison
searching.explanation: Ordering makes one side impossible after the midpoint comparison. Duplicates and negative values are allowed by this search.

searching.prompt: After the middle value is smaller than the target in inclusive-bound binary search, which update makes progress?
searching.explanation: The middle slot was already checked and is too small. Excluding it and all smaller positions leaves the possible interval.

searching.prompt: Which duplicate policy is promised by the default examples?
options: Both searches always return the final match
Linear search returns the first match; binary search may return any match
searching.explanation: Linear search stops at the first equal value in its left-to-right scan. The default binary search returns the first equal midpoint it encounters.

sorting.prompt: Is [1, 2] a correct ascending sort of [2, 1, 2]?
options: No, it loses a repeated value
Only if the sort is stable
sorting.explanation: Sorting must preserve the input’s multiplicities as well as order. The output needs two occurrences of 2.

sorting.prompt: Which insertion-sort rule preserves equal-key order?
options: Shift only strictly larger prefix values
Always put a key at index zero
sorting.explanation: Existing equal values remain before the remembered key when only strictly larger values are shifted.

sorting.prompt: Why does the demonstrated merge sort require linear auxiliary storage?
options: It saves merged values in a buffer
Every sort must use a linked list
sorting.explanation: The temporary merging buffer can hold values proportional to n. Its storage is separate from the input array.

sorting.prompt: What can happen with a final-element quicksort pivot on already sorted input?
options: Repeated highly unbalanced partitions and quadratic time
sorting.explanation: A consistently extreme pivot can leave a subproblem of size n−1. The repeated scans then add to a quadratic total.

linked-list.prompt: Deleting the only node should leave which head?
options: A link to the removed node
linked-list.explanation: After removing the only element there is no first data node. Null represents the empty chain.

linked-list.prompt: What should a new node link to before its predecessor is redirected to it?
options: An unrelated node with the same value
linked-list.explanation: Saving the old successor in new.next preserves the remaining chain before changing predecessor.next.

linked-list.prompt: Why is searching by value generally linear in a singly linked list?
options: Nodes can be followed and compared one at a time
All nodes are required to be adjacent in memory
A value directly specifies its node index
linked-list.explanation: The structure supplies next links, not a direct map from arbitrary values to nodes. A missing target can require inspecting every node.

stack.prompt: Push 3, then 8; pop once. Which value is removed?
stack.explanation: The most recently pushed value is at the top and leaves first: last in, first out.

stack.prompt: Which operation leaves a nonempty stack’s length unchanged?
stack.explanation: Peek reads the top without removing it. Pop reduces length; a successful push increases it.

options: Attempting to remove from an empty stack
stack.explanation: An empty stack has no value to remove. Use an explicit error or empty result, not an arbitrary stored-value marker.

queue.prompt: Enqueue 3, then 8; dequeue once. Which value leaves?
queue.explanation: FIFO removes the oldest arrival, 3, regardless of numeric order.

queue.prompt: Why can dequeue cost O(n) in the compact array queue?
queue.explanation: Keeping the front at index zero requires moving later values. This is a representation cost, not a requirement of FIFO.

queue.prompt: Which circular-buffer change avoids shifting on dequeue?
options: Advance the head index with wraparound
Overwrite the oldest value on every enqueue
queue.explanation: Advancing head changes the logical front without moving remaining elements. Size still distinguishes full and empty states.

bst.prompt: Which strict ordering rule does this BST use?
options: All left descendants are smaller and all right descendants larger
Only direct children need any ordering
Equal values are always inserted on the left
bst.explanation: The rule applies to whole subtrees. This module ignores duplicate insertions.

bst.prompt: For a node with two children, where is its inorder successor?
options: The smallest node in its right subtree
Any node in its left subtree
bst.explanation: Following left links from the right child reaches the smallest right-subtree value, the next value in inorder.

bst.prompt: Which traversal lists this BST’s values in ascending order?
bst.explanation: Inorder visits the smaller subtree, then the node, then the larger subtree.

bst.prompt: What limits a search route’s cost in an unbalanced BST?
options: Tree height, which may grow linearly
A guaranteed logarithmic height for every shape
The largest stored numeric value alone
bst.explanation: An unbalanced tree can become a chain. Search/insert/delete are O(h), and h may be proportional to n.

graph.prompt: Why mark a vertex as visited when it is enqueued in BFS?
options: To avoid multiple pending entries for the same vertex
graph.explanation: Two processed neighbors might discover the same vertex. Marking on enqueue prevents it from being queued again before processing.

graph.prompt: What can explain a vertex that was not visited from a chosen source?
options: It may be unreachable along allowed edges
Every source traversal must include every graph vertex
Its label is too large to compare
graph.explanation: Disconnected components and directed edge orientation can make vertices unreachable from one source.

graph.prompt: Which input must this Dijkstra lesson reject?
graph.explanation: The settled-distance guarantee requires nonnegative edges. Zero is allowed, and unreachable vertices keep infinity.

graph.prompt: A route with fewer edges must also have lower total weight. Is that guaranteed?
options: No; edge count and total weight are different costs
Yes, whenever a graph is directed
graph.explanation: BFS treats each edge as one step. Weighted shortest paths add actual edge costs, so fewer edges can still cost more.

hash-tables.prompt: With capacity 8, which bucket receives key -1 after normalization?
hash-tables.explanation: The remainder is normalized into 0..7; -1 and 7 share bucket 7.

hash-tables.prompt: What happens when an existing key is inserted with a new value?
options: Its value changes without adding another key
hash-tables.explanation: This map updates the existing entry; distinct-key count stays the same.

hash-tables.prompt: Why keep a tombstone after a probing deletion?
options: To count the removed key as live
To keep later colliding keys reachable
hash-tables.explanation: A lookup must pass a deleted slot to reach keys farther along the same probe sequence.

hash-tables.prompt: When capacity doubles, how should entries move?
hash-tables.explanation: The remainder uses the new capacity, so old bucket positions can be wrong.

hash-tables.prompt: When can expected O(1) hash lookup be a useful model?
options: Only when every bucket is full
When hashing distributes keys well and load is controlled
hash-tables.explanation: Good distribution and bounded load limit expected collisions; worst-case chains or probes may still be linear.

heaps.prompt: Which relationship must a min-heap satisfy?
options: Each parent is no greater than its children
Every adjacent array pair is sorted
All left children exceed right children
heaps.explanation: Heap ordering compares parents with children, not all neighboring array values.

heaps.prompt: During min-heap sift-down, which child should be considered first?
options: Always the left child regardless of value
The last array value regardless of parent
heaps.explanation: Choosing the smaller child allows the moved parent to satisfy both child relationships.

heaps.prompt: What is the worst-case time of bottom-up heap construction?
heaps.explanation: Most nodes can move only a short distance, so work summed by height is linear.

heaps.prompt: What happens to the suffix outside the heap during ascending heap sort?
options: It is sorted and excluded from later sifts
It must be rebuilt each step
heaps.explanation: Each maximum is moved into its final suffix position; only the remaining prefix is repaired.

heaps.prompt: How does the existing graph lesson choose Dijkstra’s next unsettled vertex?
options: This heap automatically replaces the scan
A scan using its matrix-based representation
heaps.explanation: The graph lesson uses an unsettled-vertex scan, not this priority queue.

recursion.prompt: What must a recursive case do in addition to having a base case?
recursion.explanation: A decreasing measure such as prefix length or interval size establishes progress.

recursion.prompt: Why is factorial visualization limited to n≤12?
options: The stated integer result range stays safe
recursion.explanation: 13! exceeds signed 32-bit range; the lab uses one safe contract across all example languages.

recursion.prompt: Compared with an iterative O(1)-space scan, what space does recursive prefix sum use?
recursion.explanation: Every unfinished prefix call retains a frame until its child returns.

recursion.prompt: Why can naive Fibonacci have many calls but only linear peak depth?
options: The two branches run sequentially while one path is active
The result is always computed by one call
recursion.explanation: A parent saves one child’s answer, then calls the other; total tree size differs from active path length.

recursion.prompt: What marks an empty search interval in inclusive recursive binary search?
recursion.explanation: A singleton still has one candidate; only crossed inclusive bounds mean no candidates remain.

two-pointers.prompt: In sorted pair sum, why move left when the sum is too small?
options: The current left value cannot reach the target with any remaining partner
The current right value must be removed too
two-pointers.explanation: The largest available partner already gives too small a sum for that left value.

two-pointers.prompt: Can pair sum reuse one element when left equals right?
options: Yes, every value can be used twice
No, two distinct indices are required
two-pointers.explanation: The loop condition left<right prevents using one index twice.

two-pointers.prompt: What is already correct outside reversal’s two pointers?
options: The values are in final reversed positions
two-pointers.explanation: Each swap fixes two endpoint positions before the pointers move inward.

two-pointers.prompt: What does a unique-prefix result length of 3 mean?
options: The array allocation must now have three slots
two-pointers.explanation: Physical storage remains; the suffix is not part of the logical result.

two-pointers.prompt: Why are the selected pointer scans linear?
options: Two indices always imply O(1) time
Each pointer moves monotonically and never restarts
two-pointers.explanation: There are at most a linear number of index advances under the proved movement rules.

sliding-window.prompt: What distinguishes a subarray from a general subsequence?
options: It must contain the whole array
sliding-window.explanation: A contiguous range cannot skip an interior position.

sliding-window.prompt: For [-5,-2,-8] and k=2, what is the maximum window sum?
sliding-window.explanation: The two eligible sums are -7 and -10. A singleton or empty window is not allowed.

sliding-window.prompt: Why are nonnegative values required for the selected minimum-length algorithm?
options: They make all windows the same size
Removing a left value cannot increase the sum
They guarantee every target is reachable
sliding-window.explanation: This monotonicity justifies stopping shrinking once the sum falls below target.

sliding-window.prompt: Which signed-input behavior breaks that shrinking proof?
options: Removing a negative value can increase the sum
sliding-window.explanation: An invalid current window might become valid after further shrinking, so the stopping rule is no longer justified.

sliding-window.prompt: Why does the inner shrinking loop still allow O(n) total time?
options: Left advances at most n times across the whole run
sliding-window.explanation: Each removal consumes a new position; expansions and removals are both bounded linearly.
